Hello all,

I used distance sampling to estimate the abundance and density of a mammal species on an island in southeast Asia. We had a total of 16 transects and each of the 16 transects was covered at least 4 times (4 replicates). Some of the transects had more than 4 replicates. Altogether there were 120 samples (n=120) conducted. Out of the 120 samples, 40 observations/sightings were made – cluster of animals was seen during those samples. The total study area of the island was 9.7km square.

Transect length ranged from 272m – 548m. Counting all the animals seen in clusters from the 40 observations, a total of 62 individuals were seen. The furthest sighting was one individual 50m from the transect line. Our study region was not stratified due to transect routes covering more than one habitat and the lack of available transect routes within certain habitats

Hi Debra,

I'm a little confused about what each of the rows in your spreadsheet refer to. The rows with observations in them appear to refer to single observations, as they specify a single distance and cluster size. However, given that you have multiple (between 2 and 7) rows for each transect with no observations in them, I think these blank rows might refer to individual visits. So... did you never record multiple observations of pigs on one transect in a single visit? If you did, then summing the lengths of transects surveyed in column C isn't the right thing to do (observations made in the same visit shouldn't contribute length of transect multiple times to this total). Moreover you state that each transect was surveyed at least 4 times, but that some transects were visited more often. Transects K and O appear to have been surveyed 10 times each. Is that right? I think a nicer way of showing survey effort, rather than by including lots of line with blank entries, would have been to include a 'survey effort' column for total number of visits to each transect. You would then only need blank lines (one each) for transects where no pigs were seen on any survey (just three - F, G and P).

Assuming for the now that the total length of transect surveyed is correct, you surveyed a total of 46km of transect. The largest distance recorded by you is 50m, so we may consider that the total area surveyed by you is 46 * 0.1 (50m on each side) km. So, 4.6km2. In this area, you detected 62 pigs. You have stated that the whole study area is a little more than twice this large, so assuming that you detected all the pigs within 100m, you could assume there were around 130 pigs in total. Eyeballing the distribution of distances for these observations, I would estimate that overall detection rates were somewhere between 0.5 and 0.3. If we say 0.4, and divide 130 by this number, you get an overall number for the whole area of 325 - not so different from your own most recent estimate. So, these numbers look quite sensible, provided that you have specified survey effort correctly.

As for cluster size versus detection probability, it took me a while to understand this but I think I do now. I think this relationship will be used to adjust predicted densities calculated from the detection probability graph, in order to account for (very slightly) decreasing numbers of pigs per observation as distance from the observer increases (and detection probability goes down). So, when distance = 0 (and detection probability = 100%), the average cluster size is deemed to be 2 (i.e. log10 of around 0.3 from the graph). When distance = 50m (and detection probability is near zero), average cluster size is deemed to be around 1.5 (log10 of around 0.2). That seems vaguely sensible to me. However, someone with more experience in interpreting this graph may well be able to correct or improve this explanation!

Cheers,

Mark

Debra


Mark has focused on what may be the central issue for you; have you described effort correctly such that Distance is properly accounting for survey effort.  His points regarding not having visit numbers enumerated in the data makes our interpretation more difficult.   It is also unusual to never have more than a single detection on a transect.  Recall also that for repeat visits of transects, the estimated density or abundance is an average across the time of the visits.


Now to your specific points.  (1) step back and note that the density estimates from all four of the fitted models are very similar.  The estimates of density are robust to the choice of model.  If your model fits the observed data, then you can carry on.


(2) size biased regression.  There is a video lecture and exercise that deals extensively with the issue of size bias in distance sampling.  You can view it at this URL

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation



Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.


(3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know?  I take the SE(D-hat)/(D-hat)=0.243/0.65=0.3738.  To express this as a percentage (therefore comparable with the current analysis), you would have 37.4%


Precision measurements are also discussed in the online distance sampling course:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#Measures-of-precision

Chapter 2 - Making distance sampling work
workshops.distancesampling.org
In this chapter you will learn about the assumptions that underlie distance sampling. As density/abundance metrics produced by distance sampling are estimates, measures of uncertainty (or precision) need to be associated with them.Finally, a few suggestions regarding how a distance sampling analysis might be conducted: beginning, middle and conclusion.


Without knowing more about the 2008 survey, it is difficult to know whether the two sets of results are comparable. The general interpretation of density per unit area and study area size seem reasonable.  I suspect the reason for the two surveys is to determine if boar population size has changed in the 10 years.  I'll not perform a formal test, but my suspicion is that with a CV of ~40% for the first survey and a CV of ~20% in the current survey, even with the point estimates differing substantially, a formal test incorporating uncertainty is unlikely to show a dramatic (if any) difference.


(4) Nature of your detection distances.  One of the dangers of sending data to the Distance list is that somebody will play with it.  I did exactly that to see the distribution of the 40 detection distances. 


On first look, the data look OK:


However, when splitting the data into smaller bins, the data look a bit less pretty; raising some concerns about field procedures:

The finer scale plot shows not quite half of the detections made at detection distance 0 (were surveys performed along trails cut in the jungle?) it also shows possible rounding to distances near 10m and 20m.  It is best for histograms (and detection functions) to have a shoulder (i.e. detectability should drop gradually for some distance near the transect).  That leads to better and more robust analysis.

On Wed, Sep 5, 2018 at 7:35 PM Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

Debra


Mark has focused on what may be the central issue for you; have you described effort correctly such that Distance is properly accounting for survey effort.  His points regarding not having visit numbers enumerated in the data makes our interpretation more difficult.   It is also unusual to never have more than a single detection on a transect.  Recall also that for repeat visits of transects, the estimated density or abundance is an average across the time of the visits.


Now to your specific points.  (1) step back and note that the density estimates from all four of the fitted models are very similar.  The estimates of density are robust to the choice of model.  If your model fits the observed data, then you can carry on.


(2) size biased regression.  There is a video lecture and exercise that deals extensively with the issue of size bias in distance sampling.  You can view it at this URL

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation



Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.


(3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know?  I take the SE(D-hat)/(D-hat)=0.243/0.65=0.3738.  To express this as a percentage (therefore comparable with the current analysis), you would have 37.4%


Precision measurements are also discussed in the online distance sampling course:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#Measures-of-precision

Chapter 2 - Making distance sampling work
workshops.distancesampling.org
In this chapter you will learn about the assumptions that underlie distance sampling. As density/abundance metrics produced by distance sampling are estimates, measures of uncertainty (or precision) need to be associated with them.Finally, a few suggestions regarding how a distance sampling analysis might be conducted: beginning, middle and conclusion.


Without knowing more about the 2008 survey, it is difficult to know whether the two sets of results are comparable. The general interpretation of density per unit area and study area size seem reasonable.  I suspect the reason for the two surveys is to determine if boar population size has changed in the 10 years.  I'll not perform a formal test, but my suspicion is that with a CV of ~40% for the first survey and a CV of ~20% in the current survey, even with the point estimates differing substantially, a formal test incorporating uncertainty is unlikely to show a dramatic (if any) difference.


(4) Nature of your detection distances.  One of the dangers of sending data to the Distance list is that somebody will play with it.  I did exactly that to see the distribution of the 40 detection distances. 


On first look, the data look OK:


However, when splitting the data into smaller bins, the data look a bit less pretty; raising some concerns about field procedures:

The finer scale plot shows not quite half of the detections made at detection distance 0 (were surveys performed along trails cut in the jungle?) it also shows possible rounding to distances near 10m and 20m.  It is best for histograms (and detection functions) to have a shoulder (i.e. detectability should drop gradually for some distance near the transect).  That leads to better and more robust analysis.

Hi Debra,

I'm a little confused about what each of the rows in your spreadsheet refer to. The rows with observations in them appear to refer to single observations, as they specify a single distance and cluster size. However, given that you have multiple (between 2 and 7) rows for each transect with no observations in them, I think these blank rows might refer to individual visits. So... did you never record multiple observations of pigs on one transect in a single visit? If you did, then summing the lengths of transects surveyed in column C isn't the right thing to do (observations made in the same visit shouldn't contribute length of transect multiple times to this total). Moreover you state that each transect was surveyed at least 4 times, but that some transects were visited more often. Transects K and O appear to have been surveyed 10 times each. Is that right? I think a nicer way of showing survey effort, rather than by including lots of line with blank entries, would have been to include a 'survey effort' column for total number of visits to each transect. You would then only need blank lines (one each) for transects where no pigs were seen on any survey (just three - F, G and P).

Assuming for the now that the total length of transect surveyed is correct, you surveyed a total of 46km of transect. The largest distance recorded by you is 50m, so we may consider that the total area surveyed by you is 46 * 0.1 (50m on each side) km. So, 4.6km2. In this area, you detected 62 pigs. You have stated that the whole study area is a little more than twice this large, so assuming that you detected all the pigs within 100m, you could assume there were around 130 pigs in total. Eyeballing the distribution of distances for these observations, I would estimate that overall detection rates were somewhere between 0.5 and 0.3. If we say 0.4, and divide 130 by this number, you get an overall number for the whole area of 325 - not so different from your own most recent estimate. So, these numbers look quite sensible, provided that you have specified survey effort correctly.

As for cluster size versus detection probability, it took me a while to understand this but I think I do now. I think this relationship will be used to adjust predicted densities calculated from the detection probability graph, in order to account for (very slightly) decreasing numbers of pigs per observation as distance from the observer increases (and detection probability goes down). So, when distance = 0 (and detection probability = 100%), the average cluster size is deemed to be 2 (i.e. log10 of around 0.3 from the graph). When distance = 50m (and detection probability is near zero), average cluster size is deemed to be around 1.5 (log10 of around 0.2). That seems vaguely sensible to me. However, someone with more experience in interpreting this graph may well be able to correct or improve this explanation!

Cheers,

Mark

When conducting point transects, effort is measured in terms of number of visits to the points (because the points have no length).  However, for line transects, effort is measured in terms of length.  That is why the "Survey Effort" field is of no use in your line transect survey.

To correctly record effort for transects that are of differing lengths and are visited differing numbers of times, use the product of the transect length and number of visits.  If transect 1 is of length 0.5 and is visited 4 times, effort for that transect is 2.0.  If transect 2 is of length 0.8 and is visited 6 times, effort is 4.8.

If there are 16 transects in the survey design, then 16 is the correct number of replicates.  With the elevated (incorrect) number of 120 replicates, precision of the estimates is underestimated.

Debra


Mark has focused on what may be the central issue for you; have you described effort correctly such that Distance is properly accounting for survey effort.  His points regarding not having visit numbers enumerated in the data makes our interpretation more difficult.   It is also unusual to never have more than a single detection on a transect.  Recall also that for repeat visits of transects, the estimated density or abundance is an average across the time of the visits.


Now to your specific points.  (1) step back and note that the density estimates from all four of the fitted models are very similar.  The estimates of density are robust to the choice of model.  If your model fits the observed data, then you can carry on.


(2) size biased regression.  There is a video lecture and exercise that deals extensively with the issue of size bias in distance sampling.  You can view it at this URL

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation



Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.


(3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know?  I take the SE(D-hat)/(D-hat)=0.243/0.65=0.3738.  To express this as a percentage (therefore comparable with the current analysis), you would have 37.4%


Precision measurements are also discussed in the online distance sampling course:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#Measures-of-precision

Chapter 2 - Making distance sampling work
workshops.distancesampling.org
In this chapter you will learn about the assumptions that underlie distance sampling. As density/abundance metrics produced by distance sampling are estimates, measures of uncertainty (or precision) need to be associated with them.Finally, a few suggestions regarding how a distance sampling analysis might be conducted: beginning, middle and conclusion.


Without knowing more about the 2008 survey, it is difficult to know whether the two sets of results are comparable. The general interpretation of density per unit area and study area size seem reasonable.  I suspect the reason for the two surveys is to determine if boar population size has changed in the 10 years.  I'll not perform a formal test, but my suspicion is that with a CV of ~40% for the first survey and a CV of ~20% in the current survey, even with the point estimates differing substantially, a formal test incorporating uncertainty is unlikely to show a dramatic (if any) difference.


(4) Nature of your detection distances.  One of the dangers of sending data to the Distance list is that somebody will play with it.  I did exactly that to see the distribution of the 40 detection distances. 


On first look, the data look OK:


However, when splitting the data into smaller bins, the data look a bit less pretty; raising some concerns about field procedures:

The finer scale plot shows not quite half of the detections made at detection distance 0 (were surveys performed along trails cut in the jungle?) it also shows possible rounding to distances near 10m and 20m.  It is best for histograms (and detection functions) to have a shoulder (i.e. detectability should drop gradually for some distance near the transect).  That leads to better and more robust analysis.

Hi both,

I don't have a lot of experience at analysing transect data, so the terms in which I had been considering and writing about effort were from a thoroughly point-count based perspective. Apologies if that confused you, Debra. I wasn't even aware that the windows programme Distance makes no explicit use of a visit number field for effort in transect surveys - I was (it seems wrongly) assuming that the programme would take transect length and visit number for each transect and multiply them up itself. The few line transect surveys I have analysed with Distance in the past have had equal numbers of visits per transect, so visit number hasn't been terribly relevant (at for within survey comparisons). However, Eric's explanation that you need to provide Distance with the combination of visits and individual transect length, such that survey effort = total length surveyed, make sense, and accounts for why your survey effort variable wasn't affecting the output in Distance.

Sounds like you are just about good to go! Once you have correctly specified survey effort (as described by Eric), you can safely record all your observations on separate rows (each with the correct detection distance), because now rows are equivalent to observations (not to survey visits). As stated previously, the only situation in which you need to worry about including rows to account for a survey visit is when no animals were encountered during that visit - you appear to have done this correctly from the latest screenshots you attached. Something to note is that, in Distance, an alternative approach to accounting for visits where no animals were recorded is to routinely append a 'blank' row to your dataset of observations for EVERY transect included in your survey. For transects where no animals were seen, this will make sure that the survey effort on these transects is factored into density and abundance assessments. For transects with animal data, the inclusion of a blank row will make no difference. I don't think this approach would save you much time in this instance, but it can definitely be labour saving if carrying out separate distance analyses for each one of multiple species recorded during a point count or transect survey.

Cheers,

When conducting point transects, effort is measured in terms of number of visits to the points (because the points have no length).  However, for line transects, effort is measured in terms of length.  That is why the "Survey Effort" field is of no use in your line transect survey.

To correctly record effort for transects that are of differing lengths and are visited differing numbers of times, use the product of the transect length and number of visits.  If transect 1 is of length 0.5 and is visited 4 times, effort for that transect is 2.0.  If transect 2 is of length 0.8 and is visited 6 times, effort is 4.8.

If there are 16 transects in the survey design, then 16 is the correct number of replicates.  With the elevated (incorrect) number of 120 replicates, precision of the estimates is underestimated.

Mark has focused on what may be the central issue for you; have you described effort correctly such that Distance is properly accounting for survey effort.  His points regarding not having visit numbers enumerated in the data makes our interpretation more difficult.   It is also unusual to never have more than a single detection on a transect.  Recall also that for repeat visits of transects, the estimated density or abundance is an average across the time of the visits.


Now to your specific points.  (1) step back and note that the density estimates from all four of the fitted models are very similar.  The estimates of density are robust to the choice of model.  If your model fits the observed data, then you can carry on.


(2) size biased regression.  There is a video lecture and exercise that deals extensively with the issue of size bias in distance sampling.  You can view it at this URL

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation



Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.


(3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know?  I take the SE(D-hat)/(D-hat)=0.243/0.65=0.3738.  To express this as a percentage (therefore comparable with the current analysis), you would have 37.4%


Precision measurements are also discussed in the online distance sampling course:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#Measures-of-precision

Chapter 2 - Making distance sampling work
workshops.distancesampling.org

I don't think this approach would save you much time in this instance, but it can definitely be labour saving if carrying out separate distance analyses for each one of multiple species recorded during a point count or transect survey.

Now to your specific points.  (1) step back and note that the density estimates from all four of the fitted models are very similar.  The estimates of density are robust to the choice of model.  If your model fits the observed data, then you can carry on.


(2) size biased regression.  There is a video lecture and exercise that deals extensively with the issue of size bias in distance sampling.  You can view it at this URL

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation



Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.


(3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know?  I take the SE(D-hat)/(D-hat)=0.243/0.65=0.3738.  To express this as a percentage (therefore comparable with the current analysis), you would have 37.4%
